title: Megiddo + Jezreel Valley
subtitle: Strategic landscape and period-context explorer
summary: Explore the geographic relationships among Tel Megiddo, the Jezreel Valley, Carmel, Tabor, Gilboa, and later Jezreel while keeping archaeological sites, textual events, and reconstructed strategic interpretation distinct.
disclaimer: Hotspots use existing atlas records. Period views change explanatory emphasis and camera framing; they do not reconstruct vanished architecture. Relief is real terrain only when a separately configured raster-DEM source has been verified and licensed. Without it, this remains a 2D geographic teaching view.

evidenceLegend.description: Established geographic landforms. Actual elevation rendering requires a verified DEM; the bundled fallback is flat.

evidenceLegend.description: Established archaeological site identifications already represented by the atlas.

evidenceLegend.label: Historical interpretation
evidenceLegend.description: Textual, strategic, or archaeological interpretation kept separate from directly identified physical features.

evidenceLegend.description: Exact battlefield positions, route lines, structure attribution, and other unresolved details are not converted into fake map precision.

evidenceLegend.label: Artistic reconstruction
evidenceLegend.description: Project-authored visualization used to evoke a period landscape; it is not measured archaeology or a recovered historical view.

camera.note: A cinematic regional teaching camera, not an ancient observation point.

hotspots.label: Tel Megiddo
hotspots.summary: The archaeological mound securely identified with ancient Megiddo.

whyShown.evidence: The v1 atlas records Tel Megiddo as the secure identification of ancient Megiddo.
whyShown.inference: Period views can discuss different historical contexts at the tell, but excavated phases and royal attribution remain separate interpretive questions.

hotspots.label: Jezreel Valley
hotspots.summary: A major lowland corridor and repeated arena of conflict whose broad geographic identity is secure.

whyShown.evidence: The valley is an established physical-geographic region in the existing atlas.
whyShown.inference: Calling it a strategic corridor summarizes geographic connectivity; exact ancient road alignments and army positions are not implied.

hotspots.label: Mount Tabor
hotspots.summary: A prominent Lower Galilee mountain associated with Deborah and Barak's narrative in Judges 4.

whyShown.evidence: Mount Tabor is a securely identified geographic landmark in the atlas.
whyShown.inference: The scene does not reconstruct troop positions or assume a specific historical line of sight.

hotspots.label: Mount Gilboa
hotspots.summary: The securely identified ridge associated with Saul's final battle narrative.

whyShown.evidence: Gilboa is a secure landscape identification.
whyShown.inference: The exact battlefield positions on or around the ridge are unknown and are not mapped.

hotspots.label: Mount Carmel
hotspots.summary: The geographically secure Carmel range, represented without selecting Elijah's altar site.

whyShown.evidence: The Carmel range is geographically secure.
whyShown.inference: The atlas uses a ridge-area anchor; it does not identify the later Muhraka tradition or any modern summit as the proven altar location.

hotspots.label: Jezreel / Tel Jezreel
hotspots.summary: The established site of ancient Jezreel, a northern royal center in the narratives of Ahab, Jezebel, Naboth, and Jehu.

whyShown.evidence: Tel Jezreel is securely identified with ancient Jezreel in the existing atlas.
whyShown.inference: The exact location of Naboth's vineyard and individual palace spaces cannot be recovered from the biblical text alone.

hotspots.label: 1 Kings 9:15 at Megiddo
hotspots.summary: The biblical text names Megiddo in Solomon's building levy, but assigning particular excavated monumental structures to Solomon is a separate archaeological and chronological question.

whyShown.evidence: 1 Kings 9:15 explicitly names Megiddo alongside Hazor and Gezer.
whyShown.inference: The text-site association does not by itself date every monumental gate or building phase to Solomon.
whyShown.alternatives: Competing archaeological chronologies and royal attributions must remain visible when specific structures are eventually reconstructed.

hotspots.label: Josiah at Megiddo
hotspots.summary: Kings and Chronicles place Josiah's death in connection with Pharaoh Necho II at Megiddo, but the precise encounter location is not recoverable as a map coordinate.

whyShown.evidence: Both biblical accounts connect Josiah's final campaign/death with Megiddo.
whyShown.inference: The hotspot uses the established city site as contextual geography, not an exact death location.
whyShown.alternatives: The differing narrative details in Kings and Chronicles should be discussed rather than harmonized into an invented battlefield reconstruction.

mapCamera.note: 3D teaching camera emphasizing the tel, Nahal Iron approach, and Jezreel basin. Local extrusion geometry is explanatory, not an imported excavation survey.

siteModel.label: Megiddo explanatory 3D geometry
siteModel.note: Project-authored derived display geometry centered on the identified tel. The gate volume uses research-supplied dimensions as an illustrative footprint and does not claim a surveyed coordinate or superstructure.

provenance.notes: No third-party photogrammetry is bundled in alpha.12.

reconstruction.title: Megiddo / Jezreel — animated Iron Age reconstruction
reconstruction.alt: Layered artistic reconstruction of Tel Megiddo above the Jezreel Valley with city structures and the strategic pass landscape.
reconstruction.note: Animated artistic reconstruction. The tel and regional geography are established; building elevations, gate superstructure, fields, vegetation, and skyline are illustrative and chronology remains switchable.
